strengths: Principled and practical architectural adaptation of Vision Transformers to 3D volumetric CT imaging, effectively handling cubic token growth via a two-stage local-global attention hierarchy (ViT_l and ViT_g) and explicit 3D RoPE encoding.

Comprehensive two-stage pretraining strategy that successfully bridges self-supervised visual distillation (adapted DINOv3 with 3D masking and KoLeo regularization) and report-level cross-modal alignment (SigLIP with LLM-enhanced paraphrased radiology text).
Commitment to open science by relying entirely on curated open-source CT datasets (~230k series) and pledging full release of models, training code, and pretraining recipes.

Strong and rigorous empirical evaluation across multiple downstream benchmarks, including frozen-embedding kNN classification on TumorImagingBench, zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE/Merlin, and dense semantic segmentation integrated into the nnU-Net framework (SEoMT).
weaknesses: Limited component ablation studies: while pretraining hyperparameters and segmentation finetuning settings (optimizer, crop size) are documented in Table 7, there is a lack of ablation isolating the specific impact of key design choices (e.g., 3D RoPE jittering vs. standard positional embeddings, ViT_g global aggregation vs. naive pooling, and dense patch masking ratios) on downstream tasks.

Resolution limitations in dense prediction: the SEoMT segmentation setup predicts masks at 1/4 resolution followed by trilinear upsampling; while computationally efficient and competitive on large organs, it noticeably smooths small, fine structures and low-contrast lesions (e.g., in KiTS23/LiTS) compared to dedicated heavy decoder-based architectures like nnU-Net ResEnc.

Anatomical pretraining imbalance: the curated pretraining corpus is heavily weighted towards chest CT (NLST, CT-RATE, INSPECT), which correlates with somewhat reduced margins of improvement on abdominal prognostic benchmarks (e.g., Colorectal-Liver-Metastases and KiTS).

strengths: Comprehensive and scalable foundation model framework: SPECTRE introduces a fully transformer-based architecture tailored for volumetric CT, effectively addressing token scaling and geometric anisotropy via anisotropic 3D patch embedding (16x16x8), 3D RoPE, and a two-stage local-global attention design.

Well-structured pretraining pipeline: The two-stage training scheme cleanly integrates DINOv3-style self-distillation (DINO + iBOT + KoLeo) on local crops to capture dense geometric structures, followed by SigLIP-based vision-language alignment with LLM-augmented clinical reports to inject high-level semantic grounding.

Thorough evaluation across diverse medical imaging tasks: The model is validated across three distinct evaluation protocols: frozen-embedding biomarker classification across 6 oncology cohorts, dense semantic segmentation on 4 competitive abdominal benchmarks using an encoder-only formulation (SEoMT), and zero-shot text-to-image retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin.
Open science commitment: Training exclusively on public data and committing to release pretraining recipes, code, and weights significantly benefits the 3D medical vision community.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: The core contributions primarily combine existing paradigms (DINOv3, SigLIP, local window attention, and RoPE) adapted to 3D CT rather than introducing fundamentally novel architectural or objective formulations.

Lack of detailed ablations isolating pretraining components: While Table 7 shows optimizer, deep supervision, and input crop ablations for segmentation, there is no systematic ablation quantifying the individual contributions of Stage 1 (SSL) vs. Stage 2 (VLA) across the biomarker classification and retrieval benchmarks.

Segmentation performance does not convincingly surpass standard CNN baselines: Although SPECTRE outperforms prior 3D transformer encoders, it remains behind or on par with the standard CNN-based nnU-Net and nnU-Net ResEnc L on benchmarks like AMOS-CT and WORD, largely due to predicting logits at 1/4 resolution with trilinear upsampling.

Pretraining data imbalance across anatomical regions: Approximately 88% of the pretraining cohort consists of thoracic scans (NLST, CT-RATE, INSPECT), leading to noticeable performance discrepancies between chest and abdominal prognostic tasks (e.g., lower performance on Colorectal-Liver-Metastases and NSCLC-Radiogenomics).

strengths: Principled architectural adaptation to 3D CT: The two-stage local-to-global Vision Transformer architecture (ViT_l and ViT_g) paired with anisotropic 3D patch embeddings (16x16x8) and 3D RoPE directly and effectively tackles the cubic token scaling and geometric slice anisotropy inherent to volumetric CT imaging.

Well-designed two-stage pretraining recipe: Bootstrapping dense visual features via DINOv3-style self-distillation (DINO, iBOT, KoLeo) before injecting clinical semantics with sigmoid-based vision-language alignment (SigLIP) on paired radiology reports is methodologically sound and tailored for medical data where negatives often share semantic findings.

Fully open-source pretraining using publicly available data: Pretrained on ~230k CT reconstructions sourced entirely from public repositories (NLST, CT-RATE, Merlin, etc.), ensuring reproducibility and high utility to the research community without reliance on private institutional hospital data.

Comprehensive downstream benchmarking across diverse regimes: The model is validated across three distinct evaluation protocols: frozen-feature tumor biomarker prediction (TumorImagingBench), dense 3D semantic segmentation integrated cleanly into nnU-Net, and zero-shot multimodal text-to-image retrieval.

Strong empirical performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results among volumetric CT foundation models on 4 out of 6 biomarker benchmarks, outperforms all prior 3D medical transformer backbones on multiple segmentation datasets using a lightweight decoder-free setup (SEoMT), and substantially improves zero-shot retrieval on CT-RATE.
weaknesses: Lack of isolated component ablations: While Table 7 analyzes optimizers and crop sizes on KiTS23, the paper lacks systematic ablation studies dissecting key architectural and training choices—for example, measuring the impact of the local-global hierarchy versus flat attention, the benefit of 3D RoPE over standard learned positional encodings, or a systematic ablation of SSL-only vs. VLA-only vs. combined pretraining across biomarker and retrieval benchmarks.

Absence of exact numerical tables for biomarker prediction: The quantitative results for the 11 CT foundation models on the six cancer biomarker benchmarks are presented only via radar plots (Fig. 1) and bar charts with error bars (Fig. 3) without tabular numerical metrics in either the main text or supplementary material, hindering exact benchmarking and verification.

Performance trade-off in dense segmentation: Due to the encoder-only design (SEoMT) predicting masks at 1/4 resolution with trilinear upsampling, the model still slightly lags behind the standard convolutional baseline (nnU-Net ResEnc L) across KiTS23, LiTS, and WORD, showing some limitation on fine structures and low-contrast boundaries.

Anatomical pretraining imbalance: The pretraining dataset is substantially skewed towards thoracic CT (over 130k series from NLST alone out of ~230k), which is reflected in lower relative performance and larger variance on abdominal prognostic endpoints.

strengths: Principled architectural adaptation to 3D volumetric CT: The two-stage transformer design (local ViT_l for window-level processing and global ViT_g for scan-level aggregation) combined with anisotropic 3D patch tokenization (16x16x8) and 3D RoPE effectively tackles the quadratic attention complexity and geometric anisotropy inherent to CT volumes.

Well-motivated two-stage pretraining strategy: Combining DINOv3-based self-distillation (DINO, iBOT, KoLeo) to bootstrap dense geometric features with a subsequent SigLIP vision-language alignment stage (using LLM-rewritten reports and ICD descriptions) successfully bridges dense visual representation learning with clinical semantic understanding.

Open-source and reproducible: Pretrained entirely on open-access data (~230k CT series) without relying on proprietary hospital repositories, while committing to releasing weights, preprocessing pipelines, and pretraining recipes.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors evaluate the model across diverse downstream tasks, including frozen-feature cancer biomarker classification on six benchmarks, semantic segmentation on six CT cohorts, and cross-modal zero-shot retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin, accompanied by informative ablation studies (e.g., decoder complexity, text corruptions, report lengths).
weaknesses: Ablation between Stage 1 (SSL) and Stage 2 (VLA) is only sparsely reported: While Table 8 provides a limited ablation on KiTS23 segmentation, the paper lacks a systematic breakdown showing how much Stage 2 (VLA) aids or impacts frozen feature quality on the biomarker classification benchmarks (Figure 1 / Figure 3) compared to Stage 1 alone.

Performance trade-offs on specialized tasks: While SPECTRE shows strong versatility, it trails specialized models in certain benchmarks—such as Merlin on Findings-to-image retrieval (Table 3) and CT-FM / nnU-Net ResEnc on certain organ segmentation benchmarks (Table 1, Table 9).

Limited fine-grained resolution in SEoMT: Predicting segmentation masks at 1/4 resolution with trilinear upsampling leads to pronounced performance drops on small lesions (<10 mm, Table 10). While the authors demonstrate that adding a UNETR decoder mitigates this, the native encoder-only mechanism remains structurally limited for tiny pathological targets.

strengths: Comprehensive and principled architectural framework: The proposed two-stage transformer (local ViT_l and global ViT_g) effectively tackles the cubic token scaling and memory bottlenecks of 3D CT while natively accommodating anisotropic voxel geometry via tailored patch dimensions and 3D rotary position embeddings (RoPE).

Effective two-stage pretraining recipe: Combining dense local self-supervised distillation (DINOv3-style DINO + iBOT + KoLeo) with scan-level vision-language alignment (SigLIP with LLM-rewritten reports and ICD text expansions) successfully merges fine-grained geometric grounding with high-level clinical semantics.

Extensive and rigorous benchmarking: The model is comprehensively evaluated across three diverse clinical paradigms against an impressive suite of up to 10 existing 3D CT foundation models (TumorImagingBench across 6 cancer datasets, multiple semantic segmentation benchmarks including KiTS23, LiTS, WORD, and TotalSegmentator, and zero-shot retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin).

Commitment to open science: Pretrained entirely on open-source CT data (~230k series) and fully open-sourcing the models and training code, lowering the barrier for accessible 3D foundation model research.
weaknesses: Limited pretraining ablations: While Table 8 reports an ablation comparing SSL vs. SSL+VLA on KiTS23 segmentation, there are no corresponding ablation studies quantifying the reciprocal benefits on downstream tasks—such as evaluating how much Stage 1 SSL initialization benefits zero-shot text-to-image retrieval compared to direct SigLIP pretraining from scratch, or how much Stage 2 VLA affects frozen biomarker feature representation compared to pure SSL.

Resolution limitations on fine structures: The encoder-only segmentation paradigm (SEoMT) operating at 1/4 resolution struggles significantly on small lesions (<10 mm), showing an extremely low detection rate (~1.5% - 5.4%) unless paired with a heavier UNETR-style decoder and longer training schedules, as shown in Table 10.

Anatomical pretraining imbalance: The pretraining data is heavily skewed toward chest CT (with NLST alone accounting for >132k of the ~230k scans), which correlates with lower relative gains on abdominal prognostic benchmarks (e.g., Liver-Metastases and C4KC-KiTS in Fig. 1 and Fig. 3).

Conceptual novelty is largely combinatorial: The individual technical building blocks (local-window ViT aggregation, 3D RoPE, DINOv3 multi-crop distillation, SigLIP loss, and LLM text paraphrasing) are primarily adaptations and combinations of existing methods rather than novel algorithmic paradigms.

strengths: Scale and commitment to open science: Pretraining a volumetric CT transformer on ~230k scans using exclusively publicly accessible datasets is a commendable effort that benefits the medical imaging community, particularly with the promised release of weights and pretraining code.

Principled architectural adaptation to 3D volumetric CT: The two-stage local-to-global transformer design (ViT_l and ViT_g) coupled with 3D rotary position embeddings (3D RoPE) and anisotropic patch tokenization effectively mitigates the cubically scaling token bottleneck while preserving scan-level context.

Comprehensive downstream benchmarking: The model is evaluated across diverse modalities and tasks, including cancer biomarker prediction (6 benchmarks), semantic segmentation (KiTS23, LiTS, WORD, TotalSegmentator), and zero-shot cross-modal retrieval (CT-RATE, Merlin).

Thorough supplementary ablations: The authors provide detailed ablations on decoder complexity (Linear vs. SEoMT vs. UNETR), performance on small lesions (<10 mm), text dropout/span corruption, and optimizer choices.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and methodological novelty: The pipeline is largely an assembly of existing techniques adapted to 3D CT—specifically DINOv3 (DINO + iBOT + KoLeo), SigLIP vision-language alignment, 3D RoPE, and EoMT query-based segmentation. While the engineering execution is substantial, the core scientific innovation remains somewhat incremental.

Mixed segmentation performance compared to established baselines: Despite the foundation-scale pretraining, SPECTRE (even when equipped with a UNETR decoder in Table 10) does not consistently outperform a well-tuned convnet baseline like nnU-Net ResEnc L (e.g., 87.82 vs 88.26 Dice on KiTS23). Furthermore, its detection rate on small lesions (<10 mm) is significantly lower than nnU-Net (15.12% vs 22.79%), highlighting limitations in fine-grained dense prediction.

Substantial performance gap on Findings retrieval: On the Merlin retrieval benchmark (Table 3), SPECTRE lags significantly behind Merlin on Findings-to-image retrieval (e.g., Recall@1 of 55.5% vs 77.6% at N=32, and 33.0% vs 59.4% at N=128), despite competitive performance on Impressions.

Incomplete ablation of pretraining stages: The manuscript lacks a thorough component ablation quantifying the isolated impact of Stage 1 (DINO SSL) versus Stage 2 (SigLIP VLA) across the biomarker prediction and retrieval tasks; Table 8 only explores this briefly on a single segmentation fold.

Extremely high compute barrier for re-pretraining: Pretraining on 24 Blackwell GPUs (3 DGX B200 systems) represents an industrial-level compute budget, making independent verification or end-to-end retraining challenging for most academic labs.
